strengths: Clear and well-motivated hypothesis (LLM 'suggestibility' toward unfamiliar claims) that is empirically validated with a clean preliminary study (Fig. 3) before the method is introduced.

The method is conceptually elegant: it derives the normalization scheme from a simple probabilistic coherence assumption (Eq. 1-2) and extends it with practical redundancy handling via NLI-based reweighting (wunique, wcontra).

Nice theoretical framing unifying self-consistency (generator coherence) and normalized verbalized confidence (validator coherence) as two complementary axes of coherence, which is a useful conceptual contribution beyond just the specific method.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation: multiple open- and closed-source models (Qwen3, Llama, Gemma, GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash), short-form (TriviaQA, SimpleQA) and long-form (FActScore) tasks, both gray-box and black-box settings.
Good use of standard calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, AUC) plus a novel and intuitive saturation metric (∆ε) that helps explain *why* DINCO improves calibration, not just that it does.

Useful ablations: NLI component ablation (Table 5), scaling self-consistency to 100 samples to show the gap with DINCO persists (Fig. 4), and results with verbalized numerical confidence instead of P(True) (Appendix D.1) showing robustness to confidence elicitation format.
Statistical significance testing (bootstrap/DeLong tests) is included for all main comparisons, which is often missing in this literature.
Reasonable and controlled inference budget comparison (K=10) makes the baseline comparisons fairer than many prior calibration papers.
weaknesses: The method is not truly "zero-resource"/fully black-box in the strictest sense: it depends on an external NLI model for redundancy weighting, and the ablation (Table 5) shows performance degrades substantially without it, meaning a core piece of the pipeline is an added dependency, not just a minor efficiency choice as claimed in a footnote.

Results are not uniformly superior: on Qwen3-1.7B/TriviaQA, plain NVC actually beats full DINCO on ECE and BS (0.084/0.164 vs 0.177/0.179), and in the black-box SimpleQA setting, DINCO's AUC drops sharply relative to logit-access DINCO (e.g., 0.605 vs 0.786 on GPT-4.1), suggesting the method's benefits are inconsistent, especially without token-level access.

The distractor-generation and NLI-reweighting pipeline adds nontrivial compute overhead per inference call (extra generation + NLI comparisons for each distractor), which is not clearly quantified in wall-clock/cost terms beyond the coarse "K=10 calls" accounting; a fairer cost analysis (e.g., total FLOPs/tokens or latency) would strengthen the efficiency claims.

The theoretical derivation relies on a fairly strong simplifying assumption (a single shared multiplicative bias β(C) across a mutually-exclusive claim set), and while the paper acknowledges and partially addresses violations via NLI weighting, there's no sensitivity analysis of how much this assumption breaks down (e.g., ablation on distractor count K, or quality/diversity of generated distractors).
Long-form evaluation is limited to only two models (Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-4B-IT) due to FActScore/GPT-4.1 cost, limiting generalizability claims in the long-form setting.

The preliminary study in Section 2.2 uses correctness as a coarse proxy for epistemic uncertainty, which the authors acknowledge is imperfect but do not further probe (e.g., via a more direct measure of model knowledge such as popularity/frequency statistics).

Comparisons to some very close recent related work (e.g., Chhikara 2025's distractor-based approach, RankAlign) are discussed qualitatively but not included as empirical baselines, making it harder to assess DINCO's advantage over the most similar prior methods quantitatively.

strengths: The paper is built around a clear, testable hypothesis (LLM 'suggestibility' on claims it has little information about), which is validated with a well-designed preliminary experiment (Fig. 3) before the method is introduced.

DINCO is evaluated across a reasonably broad set of settings: multiple open-source models (Qwen3-8B/1.7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B) and closed-source frontier models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash), short-form QA (TriviaQA, SimpleQA) and long-form generation (FActScore), as well as gray-box and black-box variants.

Good supporting analyses beyond the headline numbers: an ablation of the NLI reweighting component, a saturation/granularity metric (∆ε), and a scaling study showing that simply increasing self-consistency samples (even to 100) does not close the gap with DINCO at 10 calls.

The framing that unifies self-consistency (coherence across generations) and distractor normalization (coherence across validations) into a single generator-validator coherence framework is a reasonably elegant conceptual contribution.
Statistical significance testing (bootstrap for ECE/BS, DeLong test for AUC) is included, which is good practice often missing in calibration papers.
Reasonable reproducibility support: prompts, NLI model choice, and formulas are provided in detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method's core assumption—that the suggestibility bias β(c) is approximately constant across a set of mutually exclusive/related claims—is a strong, largely unverified modeling assumption; it is justified only by intuition and a single correlational preliminary study using correctness as a (acknowledged) imperfect proxy for epistemic uncertainty.

In the more realistic black-box setting (no logit access), performance degrades substantially (e.g., Table 2 shows NVC/DINCO black-box AUC dropping to ~0.60 vs. ~0.73-0.79 with logit access), suggesting the method's main benefits are contingent on having beam-search/token-probability access, which limits its practical applicability to many commercial API use cases.

Results are not uniformly favorable: DINCO does not always dominate on AUC or BS within a given model/dataset (e.g., Qwen3-1.7B NVC alone beats DINCO on BS in Table 1; MSP slightly beats DINCO on AUC for GPT-4.1 in Table 2), weakening the claim of consistent superiority.

The approach has a nontrivial computational/engineering overhead (distractor generation via beam search or prompting, an auxiliary off-the-shelf NLI model, multiple independent verbalization calls) that is only partially reflected in the "K=10 inference calls" accounting; the added complexity relative to simple verbalized confidence or self-consistency baselines is substantial and could be discussed more critically.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to closely related prior work (Tian et al. 2023 top-K prompting, Zhang et al. 2024b fidelity-based calibration, Chhikara 2025 distractor-based overconfidence study); the main differentiator (independent vs. joint prompting, plus NLI-based redundancy/contradiction weighting) is a reasonable but modest methodological advance.

Dataset scale is modest (1000 sampled questions per short-form dataset, 183 entities for FActScore), and there is no human evaluation of distractor quality/plausibility, which is central to the method's validity (poor distractors would directly bias the normalization factor).

No robustness analysis with alternative NLI models or sensitivity analysis to the number of distractors/samples (K) beyond the fixed budget of 10, leaving open questions about how sensitive results are to these hyperparameters.

Limited qualitative error analysis or discussion of failure modes (e.g., when distractor generation fails to produce genuinely mutually exclusive claims, or when the NLI model mis-scores entailment/contradiction), despite this being critical to the method's soundness.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated theoretical framing: the paper proposes a precise multiplicative bias model (f^VC = β(c) f^lat) for 'suggestibility' and derives the normalization procedure (DINCO) directly from this model, grounding the method in a testable hypothesis rather than ad hoc heuristics.

The preliminary study (Fig. 3) convincingly validates the core hypothesis that total verbalized confidence over distractors is higher for incorrect (epistemically uncertain) answers than correct ones, providing empirical support before the method is introduced.

Thorough and broad experimental evaluation: short-form (TriviaQA, SimpleQA) and long-form (FActScore biography generation) tasks, open-source (Qwen3, Llama, Gemma) and closed-source (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash) models, both gray-box (logit access) and strict black-box settings, and multiple confidence formats (P(True) and verbalized numerical confidence in the appendix).

Strong set of baselines (VC, K-VC, MSP, SC, SC-VC) and careful controlled comparison at a fixed inference budget (K=10), plus statistical significance testing (bootstrap for ECE/BS, DeLong test for AUC).

Useful additional analyses: a novel saturation metric (Δε) that explains why DINCO improves usability/granularity of confidence beyond calibration error alone, a scaling experiment showing DINCO at 10 calls beats self-consistency even at 100 samples, and an ablation isolating the contribution of the NLI-based reweighting.

Good positioning relative to related work (generator-validator disagreement, coherence norms, human suggestibility literature), with a thoughtful discussion connecting LLM behavior to psychological literature on human probability judgments and suggestibility.

The method is practically appealing given it is zero-resource/training-free and works in both gray-box and black-box regimes, with reasonable technique for pseudo-beam search when logits are unavailable.
weaknesses: The gains from combining SC and NVC into full DINCO are inconsistent: for Qwen3-1.7B on TriviaQA (Table 1), DINCO actually has worse ECE (0.177) and BS (0.179) than NVC alone (0.084, 0.164), with only AUC improving; this undercuts the paper's central claim that integrating both coherence dimensions is uniformly beneficial, and is not clearly discussed or explained in the text.

The method is not strictly 'zero-resource' as it depends on an off-the-shelf NLI model, and the ablation (Table 5) shows this component is critical (ECE roughly doubles without it) — this dependency and its sensitivity (e.g., to NLI model choice/quality) is not explored further.

In the black-box setting (no logit access), DINCO's AUC is noticeably weaker than several baselines (e.g., 0.605 vs. MSP's 0.800 on GPT-4.1/SimpleQA), suggesting the practical benefit of the method is substantially reduced without token-probability access, which is a meaningful limitation for the many real-world deployments that only expose black-box APIs.

The inference and computational overhead of DINCO (generating and independently validating multiple distractors, plus pairwise NLI computations for uniqueness/contradiction weighting, plus self-consistency sampling) is not quantified in wall-clock or cost terms beyond the abstract 'K=10 calls' framing; a more detailed cost/latency comparison against baselines at matched compute would strengthen practical claims.
The long-form evaluation is limited to only 2 models (Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-4B-IT) and 183 entities due to GPT-4.1 FActScore evaluation cost, limiting generality of long-form conclusions.

The distractor generation and redundancy-correction pipeline (minimal pairs via beam search/prompting, NLI-based downweighting) has several moving parts and hyperparameters (number of distractors, beam search settings, NLI thresholds) whose sensitivity is not systematically studied beyond the single ablation removing NLI entirely.

LLM-as-judge is used for short-form correctness labeling and FActScore relies on LLM-based decomposition/verification; while agreement checks are reported for the former, potential judge biases could interact with the confidence calibration metrics in ways not fully explored.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated hypothesis (LLM suggestibility under epistemic uncertainty) that is empirically validated in a preliminary study before the method is introduced, giving the approach a principled grounding rather than being purely ad hoc.

The method (DINCO) is conceptually elegant: it unifies two previously separate lines of work (self-consistency as generation-side coherence, and normalized verbalized confidence as validation-side coherence) via the generator-validator disagreement framing, which is a nice theoretical contribution beyond just an empirical trick.

Extensive experimentation across short-form (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, BioASQ) and long-form (FactScore) tasks, multiple open-source models (Qwen3 1.7B/8B/32B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B) and frontier closed models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash), and both gray-box and black-box settings, demonstrating broad applicability.

Strong set of ablations and robustness checks: NLI model choice, inference budget split, P(True) vs numerical confidence, one-step vs two-step distractor generation/validation, and a FLOP-controlled scaling analysis showing that scaling self-consistency alone cannot match DINCO.

Introduction of a novel and useful diagnostic (confidence saturation, quantified via the ∆ε metric) that provides additional insight into why verbalized confidence is unreliable beyond standard calibration metrics.
Statistical significance testing (bootstrap CIs for ECE/BS, DeLong test for AUC) is included, which is often missing in calibration papers and strengthens the empirical claims.

Good engagement with related work, clearly distinguishing DINCO's independent-prompting approach from prior joint-prompting/top-k confidence elicitation methods, with a clear rationale for why independent prompting better exposes incoherence.
weaknesses: In the black-box setting (no logit access), DINCO's AUC sometimes falls substantially below simpler baselines (e.g., GPT-4.1 on SimpleQA: DINCO_black-box AUC 0.605 vs. SC-VC 0.761 and SC 0.750), yet this notable degradation is only briefly acknowledged in the main text without deeper analysis of why coherence-based normalization fails to help ranking in this regime.

The final combination f^DINCO = 1/2 f^SC + 1/2 f^NVC is a fixed, unweighted average without theoretical justification for equal weighting or exploration of a learned/adaptive combination; the robustness check on budget splits (Appendix D.4) partially compensates but the weighting formula itself is not ablated.

The theoretical derivation in Section 2.1 rests on a fairly strong simplifying assumption (that the suggestibility bias β(c) is approximately constant across a mutually-exclusive claim set), which is plausible but not directly verified, only indirectly supported through downstream calibration results.

Reliance on an external off-the-shelf NLI model for redundancy/contradiction weighting introduces a dependency whose quality is critical (shown by the large ECE degradation in the NLI ablation), and while the authors argue NLI is a 'solved' task, no analysis is given of cases where NLI errors specifically harm calibration (e.g., under domain shift or subtle claims).

Additional inference cost (32% more FLOPs than self-consistency in the main setup, reducible to 10% with the one-step variant) may still be a practical barrier for some deployment settings, and cost-accuracy tradeoffs against stronger, more expensive baselines (e.g., higher-budget SC-VC or ensembles) are not as thoroughly explored as the SC scaling comparison.

Some baseline comparisons are mixed or inconsistent across metrics/settings (e.g., MSP sometimes wins on AUC while losing badly on ECE), and the paper's narrative sometimes emphasizes DINCO's wins while somewhat downplaying these inconsistencies, which could benefit from more balanced discussion.

The method's effectiveness depends on the generator LLM being able to produce plausible, diverse, minimal-pair distractors; while Appendix C.1 provides supportive analysis, there is no systematic failure-mode analysis of what happens when distractor generation is poor (e.g., for very obscure or highly technical claims) beyond the aggregate BioASQ result.

strengths: Well-motivated hypothesis (suggestibility bias) supported by a clear preliminary empirical study (Fig. 3, extended in Appendix D.1) showing higher total verbalized confidence on incorrectly answered questions.

Extensive experimental coverage across short-form (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, BioASQ) and long-form (FactScore biography) tasks, multiple open-source (Qwen3 family, Llama, Gemma) and closed-source (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash) models, and both P(True) and numerical verbalized confidence formats.

Thorough ablation studies (NLI model choice robustness, inference budget split, one-step vs. two-step distractor generation/validation, black-box vs. logit-access settings) that add credibility to the robustness claims.

The conceptual framing unifying self-consistency (generation coherence) and normalized verbalized confidence (validation coherence) via generator-validator disagreement is a reasonably elegant contribution.
Useful analysis of confidence saturation as a distinct, underexplored failure mode beyond standard calibration error, with a concrete metric (Δε) to quantify it.
Efficiency analysis (FLOP counts, scaling self-consistency to 100 samples) convincingly shows that simply scaling the baseline cannot match DINCO's calibration.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation (Eqs. 1-2) rests on strong, loosely justified assumptions—that bias β(c) is approximately constant across a distractor set and that the model's latent confidence is coherent—which are asserted rather than rigorously validated; the ad hoc max(1, β(C)) correction further suggests the formal model is a rough heuristic rather than a principled derivation.

Empirical gains are inconsistent: DINCO is not always the best method (e.g., MSP beats DINCO on ECE/AUC in some TriviaQA and SimpleQA settings; NVC alone sometimes has better AUC than DINCO on FactScore), and the black-box variant of DINCO on SimpleQA underperforms baselines like MSP/SC on AUC, weakening the generality of the claimed improvements.

The method's validity partly hinges on the generator LLM producing high-quality, diverse distractors and then judging them—raising circularity concerns, since the same (potentially miscalibrated) model both proposes and evaluates the alternative claims; the paper's defense of this (Appendix C.1) is largely qualitative rather than rigorously tested (e.g., no comparison using a genuinely independent/stronger distractor generator).

Reliance on correctness as a proxy for epistemic certainty in the core motivating study (Section 2.2) is acknowledged as noisy but is never more rigorously validated (e.g., via human-annotated epistemic uncertainty labels), leaving the central hypothesis only indirectly supported.

Despite claims of being "zero-resource," the method depends on an external NLI model, which the paper's ablations show is critical to performance (Table 5); this is a nontrivial resource dependency, particularly in specialized domains (e.g., biomedical) where a lightweight general-purpose NLI model's reliability is not deeply validated beyond one additional benchmark.

The core idea (independently eliciting confidence over multiple candidate answers and normalizing) is conceptually close to prior multi-answer verbalized confidence approaches (Tian et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2024b); the novelty is primarily in the independent-elicitation framing and NLI-based redundancy weighting, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

DINCO incurs consistently higher inference cost than several baselines (32% more than SC in the two-step version), and while the one-step variant reduces this, it does so with a measurable calibration cost (Table 16), suggesting a nontrivial cost-performance trade-off that is not fully resolved.
Long-form evaluation is limited to only two models (Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-4B-IT) due to FactScore evaluation cost, limiting confidence in generalization of long-form results across model scales/families.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated hypothesis (LLM 'suggestibility' under epistemic uncertainty) that is first validated empirically before the method is introduced, giving the approach a principled grounding rather than being purely heuristic.

The DINCO method is technically well-formulated, with a clean derivation (multiplicative bias model, normalization by distractor confidence) and a sensible mechanism (NLI-based reweighting) for handling redundant/non-contradictory distractors.

Extensive and diverse experimental evaluation: multiple open-source model families/scales (Qwen3-1.7B/8B/32B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B) and frontier closed models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash), short-form QA (TriviaQA, SimpleQA), long-form generation (FactScore biography), and an additional domain-transfer test (BioASQ biomedical QA), plus both white-box and black-box (no logit access) settings.

Strong supporting analyses beyond headline numbers: a novel saturation metric (Δϵ) explaining why DINCO improves usability of confidence scores, a compute-controlled scaling study showing DINCO at 10 calls beats self-consistency at 100, ablations of the NLI component and NLI model choice, budget-split robustness analysis, and a cost-reduced one-step variant.

Significance testing (bootstrap/DeLong tests) is used to support comparisons rather than relying on point estimates alone, and prompts/methodological details are thoroughly documented in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

The paper situates itself clearly relative to related work on generator-validator disagreement, self-consistency, and joint multi-answer prompting, articulating a clear conceptual distinction (independent vs. joint elicitation) that is also empirically tested.
weaknesses: DINCO's advantage is not uniform across all metrics/settings (e.g., MSP sometimes wins on AUC, SC sometimes wins on AUC/Pearson-r in the FactScore Qwen3-8B setting), so the paper's claims of consistent superiority are only partially supported and require some cherry-picking of which metric to emphasize.

The approach depends on an external NLI model and on beam search/pseudo-beam search for generating minimal-pair distractors; the black-box (no logit access) variant of DINCO performs noticeably worse than the white-box version, suggesting the practical method is less robust when only text I/O is available.

The core assumption that suggestibility bias β(c) is approximately constant across a mutually-exclusive claim set is a strong simplifying assumption that is not directly validated, only indirectly supported via downstream calibration results.

DINCO incurs meaningfully higher inference cost than the strongest baseline (SC), and although a one-step variant reduces this, the reported savings (32%→10% overhead) still add non-trivial cost and engineering complexity (extra NLI scoring, distractor generation prompts) relative to simpler baselines.

Dataset sizes (1000 sampled questions per short-form dataset, 183 entities for FactScore) are moderate, and correctness-as-proxy-for-epistemic-certainty in the preliminary study (Section 2.2) is acknowledged as noisy, somewhat weakening the strength of the core empirical claim underlying the method's motivation.
